I have opened a lot of kick-off calls, and I always ask for the same thing. Please keep the round short. One minute each, ninety seconds at most, because on a project like this there are usually fifteen people on the line. The mistake I hear most often is that somebody gives only a job title. Senior manager, lead engineer, technical director. Nobody on the call knows what that means in another country, in another office, with another org chart. So I ask for three things instead. First, your role, in normal words. Second, how big your team is. And third, what you are working on right now, this week, not in general. When people do that, the call starts well, and everybody knows who to write to on Friday.

I am a process engineer, and I have been in Houston for about nine years. In general, what I do is design process plants for the food and chemical industries. That is my job, every year, every project. But that is not what people on a call usually need to know. What they need to know is what I am doing this month, and this month I am working on a joint project with our Brazilian office. We are splitting the work: they are taking the buildings, and we are taking the process equipment. I say both things when I introduce myself, because the two are different. My job explains why I am on the call. My current task explains what you can ask me about on Thursday.

Welcome to the group. This recording explains how our offices fit together, because the structure surprises people in their first month. The headquarters are in Stockholm. Stockholm decides the standards, the software we buy, and the big commercial questions. Everything else happens in the subsidiaries. Each subsidiary keeps its own client base, its own disciplines, and its own way of running a project, and that is on purpose. A plant in Brazil is not built the way a plant in Finland is built. The most common source of confusion, in our experience, is not the language. It is the job titles. The same title means a different level in each country, so when you introduce yourself on a project call, say what you actually do, and how many people report to you. That one sentence saves everybody a lot of guessing.
